_about: The harder half of the M14 context-loss measurement. Eight items, all of them CONCEPTS rather than tokens: nothing here is a ticket id or a hex sha that a model either reproduces verbatim or does not. Each item therefore carries a paraphrase-tolerant alias set, so a session that genuinely retained the idea scores as recall even when it re-words it. Run this alongside case-01: the spread between the two scores is the measurement that matters — case-01 measures token survival, case-02 measures meaning survival, and a large gap says compaction kept the gist and dropped the specifics.
_kind_mapping: Same mapping as case-01: the scorer knows fact / decision / file only, so CONSTRAINTS sit in `decisions` tagged `constraint: true`. No `constraints` array — parseContextSnapshot would silently drop it.
_alias_rule: matchTargets() ORs `text` with every alias, after normalizeForMatch() lowercases and collapses whitespace, and matching is substring containment against the concatenated answers. Aliases are therefore kept SHORT and atomic — a long alias is a conjunction the model has to reproduce whole, which defeats the point. Adding an alias can only ever raise the score, so an alias must be something that genuinely means the item and nothing else.
_seed_field: `text` is the match key; `seed` is the natural sentence the RUNBOOK puts in the seed prompt. The scorer never reads `seed`; every `seed` contains its item's `text` verbatim, which the CLI test asserts.

probes.question: Remind me of the three numeric policies I gave you at the start: the repeat thresholds, the ledger cap, and the subagent limits.
How did we decide recall would be judged, and why not the obvious alternative?
What is the rule about a hook that crashes, and what do we do with any behaviour that differs from the original?
What is our stance on context survival across compaction, and which module implements it?
